taskA.text: The paper reports the tasks are "using few-shot prompting" [S180] and evaluations use mean ± 95% CI [S199]. I could not locate details on the specific model, number of runs, or a 200-review pilot in the sections provided. How, if at all, would the inclusion of such methodological details affect your assessment of the experimental findings?

judge_raw.issues: S180 is cited, and it says an LLM was used with few-shot prompting. The quote slightly misrepresents it, since 'tasks are using few-shot prompting' is not the exact wording. 'Evaluations use mean ± 95% CI' overstates S199, which only says the values are mean ± 95% CI. The copilot says it could not locate the model, run counts, or the pilot but does not name the sections it checked, which the rules require. The '200-review pilot' is the reviewer's claim, and the copilot neither checked nor reported whether the paper mentions it. The question is hypothetical and somewhat leading, because it presumes those details would affect the assessment. It is also loosely framed around 'inclusion' of details whose absence was not established. There is no evaluative language and no endorsement of 'weak', which is good.

judge_norm.issues: The restatement of [S180] paraphrases 'tasks are using few-shot prompting' awkwardly. It is mostly grounded. Saying 'evaluations use mean ± 95% CI' slightly overextends [S199], which only says values are mean ± CI. The absence statement doesn't name the specific sections checked ('in the sections provided' is vague), which violates the rule. [S180] says 'an LLM' without naming one; noting this would have directly addressed the reviewer's claim. The question is hypothetical and steers toward the reviewer's 'weak' assessment ('affect your assessment'). It could be more open and useful, e.g., asking what evidence would show whether the pilot exists. No praise or criticism of the reviewer appears. There is no evaluative language in the copilot's own voice.

taskA.text:
The paper states it is a position paper arguing for an AI-augmented peer-review ecosystem as an urgent priority [S2-S4, S28]. It proposes specific AI roles [S4, S29], a research agenda [S6, S29, S30], and illustrates experiments [S29, S177-S195]. I could not locate a direct comparison to prior position papers in the related work section [S62-S79] that would establish its novelty relative to them.

Given that the assessment of novelty and the decision are yours to make, what specific aspects of the paper's contributions, if any, do you find most distinctive?

judge_raw.issues: No cited sentence texts were provided, so none of the claims can be verified. The range tags (S2-S4, S62-S79, S177-S195) are broad and look padded. The 'I could not locate a direct comparison to prior position papers... that would establish its novelty' line frames an absence as bearing on novelty, which implies a judgment. It also presumes such a comparison is needed, and it names the related-work range rather than the sections checked. The decline is acceptable, but it comes only after an implicit lean against novelty rather than briefly up front. The question is open and uses 'if any', but 'most distinctive' presupposes the paper has distinctive aspects and nudges the reviewer toward a novelty framing. The prose is near the limit but acceptable.

judge_norm.issues: Verdict request: the turn defers the decision to the reviewer, but only in a clause tucked into the question rather than as a brief upfront statement. Neutrality: the 'I could not locate' line is framed around what would 'establish its novelty', which hints at a novelty gap and leads the reviewer. It also names only one section checked. Grounding: the tag ranges [S2-S4] and [S29, S177-S195] overreach. S5 was not provided, and the ranges are broad dumps rather than precise citations. Citing S6 for 'research agenda' is fine. Question quality: 'most distinctive' carries a mild presupposition despite the 'if any' hedge, and it nudges toward a novelty judgment, though it remains a single open question. Concision: prose is roughly 80 words, which is acceptable.

taskA.text: The paper's illustrative experiments used ICLR corpora and reported recall metrics [S180-S185] and rating prediction MAE/RMSE with 95% CIs [S188-S195]. I could not locate details on the number of experimental runs or the specific LLM used, and I could not locate mention of a "200-review pilot" in Sections 1, 6, or 9. In your view, how, if at all, does the lack of such methodological specifics affect the interpretation of the experimental results?

judge_raw.issues: Cited tags [S180-S185] and [S188-S195] are range citations, and no sentence texts were provided to verify them. The claims about ICLR corpora, recall metrics, MAE/RMSE and 95% CIs therefore cannot be checked and may be invented. The question uses the phrase 'the lack of such methodological specifics', which presupposes an absence the copilot only says it could not locate. The phrase also leans toward the reviewer's 'weak' framing. The 'I could not locate' statements do name sections (1, 6, 9), but it is unclear whether the experimental-setup sections were checked. The turn has no neutral restatement of the reviewer's view. The 'made up' accusation is handled by the absence check alone, without separating it from the claim that the paper says nothing about runs or model. Prose is under 90 words. No evaluative words appear in the copilot's own voice.

judge_norm.issues: The phrase 'the lack of such methodological specifics' presupposes the specifics are absent rather than only not located, and it frames the question around the reviewer's negative view. This is leading. The question should be open, e.g. 'what, if anything, would you need...'. Groundedness problems: range tags [S180-S185] and [S188-S195] are used in place of individual tags. 'Illustrative experiments' is not supported by any cited sentence. 'Recall metrics' fits [S181] but is tagged to the whole range. No cited sentence mentions 95% CIs; [S189] shows ± values only. The 'I could not locate' statements name Sections 1, 6 and 9, but whether those sections cover the experiments is unclear. [S188] says 'the model' without naming one, so the not-located claim is plausible. There is no restatement of the reviewer's words. The copilot did not endorse the 'made up' accusation, which is good. The turn stays within the word limit.

taskA.text: The paper states its position is that AI-augmented peer review must become an urgent research priority and calls for community action to develop an ecosystem [S0, S28]. To assess novelty, one could examine the specific proposals and experiments detailed in Sections 4-6 [S29, S80-S210]. What specific aspects of the proposed AI ecosystem or research agenda, if any, do you find to be new relative to existing work discussed in Section 3 [S62-S79]?

judge_raw.issues: The reviewer explicitly asked for a verdict on novelty and acceptance. The copilot never stated that the assessment is the reviewer's to make; it only redirected implicitly. The phrase 'To assess novelty, one could examine...' gives procedural steering in the copilot's own voice. The cited sentence texts were not provided, so none of the claims can be verified. The tags look broad or possibly invented ranges (S80-S210, S62-S79), with sections asserted without support. The question carries a mild presupposition ('what specific aspects... do you find to be new'), though 'if any' softens it. It also adds a framing ('relative to existing work discussed in Section 3') that the paper's text has not been shown to support.

judge_norm.issues: Never explicitly says the novelty/accept assessment is the reviewer's to make; it skips the required brief decline and slides into advising how to 'assess novelty'. The accept question is ignored entirely. Range citations S80-S210 and S62-S79 are overly broad: S210 is a table fragment, and many sentences in the range were not supplied. S0 alone doesn't state the 'urgent research priority' claim; S28 partially supports it. The question contains 'if any' but also asks 'what specific aspects... do you find to be new', which is slightly leading. It also frames comparison against Section 3 only. Prose is about 70 words, which is fine.
